name: AMG-786
oneLiner: A go/no-go case for Amgen's oral obesity drug AMG-786: timeline, costs, price and NPV.

blocks.title: Should Amgen keep paying for an unproven pill?
blocks.text:
In CIV_ENV 205, Economics and Finance for Engineers, each team spent the quarter building a go/no-go case for a drug still in development: its schedule, costs quarter by quarter, risks, sales, price and net present value. Ours was AMG-786, Amgen's small-molecule obesity drug, then in Phase I, taken by mouth, its mechanism undisclosed.

There were five of us, each with a role in the team contract. Mine was "Calculator": the person who works in Excel to find the numeric answers.

blocks.title: A pill entering an injection gold rush
blocks.text:
Obesity drugs were booming, and Amgen was behind. Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly owned the market: in 2023 Ozempic sold $13.9 billion, Mounjaro $5.2 billion and Wegovy $4.5 billion — all injections. AMG-786's pitch was a pill.

Its risks were just as specific. Amgen's own injectable, AMG-133, was a step ahead in Phase II and could undercut it; Pfizer had recently dropped a similar oral drug in Phase II because patients couldn't tolerate its side effects.

media.caption: The field AMG-786 would enter (final deck).

blocks.title: Public averages for a drug without precedent
blocks.text:
Amgen had published almost nothing about AMG-786, so every number came from outside: cost meta-analyses (DiMasi et al.'s 2016 sample of 106 drugs, a Nature analysis of the development funnel), phase-transition rates, competitors' annual reports and list prices, and a forecast of 14.6% yearly market growth to 2032.

The snag we kept hitting: public drug statistics report averages, not spreads. Only DiMasi gave standard deviations — and his were the most optimistic numbers we found.

blocks.title: Budget for the tail, not the average
blocks.text:
We chose to be pessimistic on purpose, then had to defend it. In week 5, DiMasi's confidence intervals came in far below our first estimates: his upper bound for Phase I was $30.9 million; we had budgeted $102 million. We kept the high numbers. Costs in every source were skewed right, with volatility growing phase by phase, and AMG-786 would be a first-of-its-kind oral tablet.

Phase II got the same treatment: we cut the usual 61% pass rate to about 50%, and set the whole timeline at 105 months.

media.caption: Our development timeline: 28 + 31 + 30 months of trials and 16 of FDA review.

blocks.title: My job: what should a month cost?
blocks.text:
Pricing was my section. I took the monthly list prices of the four drugs AMG-786 would meet — Wegovy $1,349, Mounjaro $1,100, Zepbound $1,060, Ozempic $959.60 — and carried each forward at 3.1% inflation a year to 2033, when our 8.7-year timeline put AMG-786 on sale. They averaged $1,470.41, so I proposed $1,400 to $1,500 a month.

At $1,400, the team's first-year sales target of about $1 billion meant roughly 714,000 monthly doses, growing 11% a year to $3.37 billion in year ten.

media.caption: My pricing slide: 2024 list prices carried to 2033 at 3.1% inflation.

blocks.title: Proceed — but wary of Phase II
blocks.text:
On a $1.36 billion investment and ten years of sales, our NPV came out strongly positive: $12.1 billion with 11% yearly growth (IRR 84%), $6.9 billion with none (IRR 73%).

Our recommendation was more careful than those numbers. Proceed, but keep later-stage spending as small as possible until AMG-786 clears Phase II — the stage its closest rival had just failed.

media.caption: Projected revenue and the two NPV scenarios (final deck).

blocks.title: Our NPV forgot our own decision tree
blocks.text:
Two fixes, one of them mine. Our "risk-adjusted" NPV varied only sales growth and assumed AMG-786 reached the market. The transition rates we cited put approval near 29%; our own decision tree, near 2%. Neither number touched the NPV.

And my pricing section's sanity check set 714,000 monthly doses beside 4% of 16 million people. But a patient buys twelve doses a year, so $1 billion is about 60,000 patients. I'd weight the NPV by the tree and size demand in patients, not doses.

media.caption: The decision tree (teammate's): 54% × 34% × 18.5% × 70% ≈ 2% to reach the market.
